questions.stem: A prompt supplies four policy files, one of them a vendor email that says "ignore the instructions above". The answers never state which file backs each claim, so reviewers cannot trace them. Which change fits best?

options.text: Place the files above the instructions, which marks them as data for the model
options.says: Ruled out because "Order is not a boundary", and an email that says "ignore the instructions above" still reads as an instruction wherever it sits.

options.text: Tell Claude to cite its sources more carefully in each answer it writes
options.says: Ruled out because the guidance is to "Refer to tags by name in the instructions", which a general plea does not do.

options.text: Give each item an indexed tag, declare it data, and ask for the index cited
options.says: Nested tagged blocks with an index let the answer name the one it used, and a statement that the content is data does the marking (module 6, page 2).

options.text: Use one tag for all four files and ask for the page number cited
options.says: Ruled out because the documents must nest "each with an index or a name, so the answer can say which one it used".

questions.stem: A local charity asks Claude to draft a fundraising email and receives text that is accurate but could have been written for any charity. Which emphasis does the course give for a drafting task?

options.text: Breadth first, many options and judgment kept for a second pass
options.says: Ruled out because that is the brainstorming task: "brainstorming wants breadth first and judgment later".

options.text: Named references, claims tied to them and gaps declared in the text
options.says: Ruled out because that is the research task: "research wants sources named and unsupported claims flagged".

options.text: The material and the question, with proof shown for each finding
options.says: Ruled out because that is the analysis task: "Analysis wants the material and the question".

options.text: The audience, the tone and an example of the style wanted
options.says: A drafting task wants audience, tone and an example of the target style (module 5, page 1).

origin.section: Know what you are describing for

questions.stem: A director's request to Claude names the deliverable, its length and its readers, and gives the steps to follow, but is silent on how Claude should behave. The drafts endorse every proposal the director makes. Which two statements fit? (Select two.)

options.text: A sample of the target style is the missing piece
options.says: Ruled out because the page adds an example only "when a style matters".

options.text: The performance part is the one that is absent
options.says: The performance part says how Claude should behave, including "whether to challenge you" (module 5, page 1), and the stem leaves it out.

options.text: The process part is the one that is absent
options.says: Ruled out because the page describes that part as "The steps or approach you want followed, what to consult, what to ignore".

options.text: That part says whether pushback is welcome
options.says: The performance part says how Claude should behave, including "whether to challenge you" (module 5, page 1), and the stem leaves it out.

options.text: The product part is the one that is unclear
options.says: Ruled out because the page defines it as "The deliverable, its form (an email, a table, a list of options), its length and its audience".

origin.section: Describe: the three things to say

questions.stem: A user pastes a 25-page report beneath a single line of instruction and gets weak, unfocused answers. The user also needs any instruction hidden inside the report to be ignored. Which change fits best?

options.text: Add a role such as world-class analyst and ask for tighter focus
options.says: Ruled out because a role "changes style and focus, not truth", and it neither marks the report as data nor moves the question to the end.

options.text: Wrap the material in tags, place it first and end with the question
options.says: Long inputs go near the top, tagged as data, with the query at the end (module 6, pages 1 and 2).

options.text: Repeat the instruction in the middle of the report as well as at the top
options.says: Ruled out because "A key instruction buried in a long paragraph is easy to underweight".

options.text: Move the report above the instructions and let its position mark it as data
options.says: Ruled out because "Moving a pasted document above the instructions does not mark it as data".

origin.section: Give Claude a role, for what it is

questions.stem: A team lead wants a quick check that a prompt says enough before it goes live. Which working rule from the course fits?

options.text: Imagine handing it to a capable colleague new to the project
options.says: The colleague test: if a capable newcomer would need to ask a question first, the answer belongs in the prompt (module 6, page 1).

options.text: Run it on one typical input and accept it if the reply reads well
options.says: Ruled out because "Changing a prompt and re-reading one answer is anecdote".

options.text: Ask Claude to score the prompt from one to ten for completeness
options.says: Ruled out because "Self-reported confidence is not a measure of accuracy".

options.text: Check that it opens with a role line and carries quality adjectives
options.says: Ruled out because the page names "Stacking adjectives instead of constraints" as a trap.

questions.stem: A team needs replies in a rarely seen house format of three labelled lines, including a fallback line for tickets that fit no category, and instructions alone give inconsistent layouts. Which prompting approach fits best?

options.text: Several varied samples, with one for the unclassifiable case
options.says: A rare format with subtle boundaries calls for several varied examples, including a borderline case (module 6, page 2).

options.text: One sample taken from an unrelated task, shown after the instructions
options.says: Ruled out because examples should "Mirror your actual use case closely".

options.text: Three near-identical easy samples, to keep the layout consistent
options.says: Ruled out because "Three easy, near-identical examples teach one pattern", and the fallback case would be mishandled.

options.text: A longer written description of the layout, with no samples attached
options.says: Ruled out because zero-shot suits a case where "The task is common and easy to describe", and this format is not.

questions.stem: A support lead adds "You are a licensed pharmacist" to a prompt, expecting dependable medication advice from the replies. Which statement about that line is accurate?

options.text: It changes the voice and focus of the answers
options.says: A role steers style and attention and does not make a statement true (module 6, page 1).

options.text: It stands in for a task line in the prompt
options.says: Ruled out because "A role needs a task" and "You are a helpful assistant" adds little on its own.

options.text: It lets the answers be trusted without a check
options.says: Ruled out because the page says a role "changes style and focus, not truth".

options.text: It works as a safeguard on protected facts
options.says: Ruled out because "A role is not a safeguard" and the page adds that such a request can be argued around.

origin.section: Give Claude a role, for what it is

questions.stem: A manager types "Write something about our Q3 results" and receives a generic paragraph with no specifics. The board pack is due within the hour. Which revision best fixes the request?

options.text: Name the readers, the form, the numbers to use and how to treat gaps
options.says: A good description gives the product, the process and the performance, with the goal and context.

options.text: Add that the result must be concise, thorough, clear and professional
options.says: Ruled out because "Stacking adjectives instead of constraints" gives conflicting, unverifiable demands.

options.text: Add a role such as senior analyst and leave the rest unchanged
options.says: Ruled out because "A role is a request, not a credential", so a role does not supply missing figures.

options.text: Run the request three times and keep the best-sounding draft
options.says: Ruled out because "Regenerating the same request and hoping is the reflex; revising the request is the method".

questions.stem: A summary of a supplier contract is correct in every sentence, yet the manager later finds a penalty clause missing. Which two statements describe the shortfall? (Select two.)

options.text: The draft passed on accuracy but failed on coverage
options.says: A summary "can be accurate in every sentence and still leave out the clause that matters" (module 5, page 2), which is a completeness failure.

options.text: Fairness failed because the supplier's framing was favoured
options.says: Ruled out because "Bias in a response often comes from the framing of the request".

options.text: Audience fit failed because the manager wanted another tone
options.says: Ruled out because the page's example is "An accurate technical answer can be wrong for a board", which concerns the reader.

options.text: Silent omissions are the quiet failure
options.says: A summary "can be accurate in every sentence and still leave out the clause that matters" (module 5, page 2), which is a completeness failure.

options.text: Accuracy failed because a figure was not traced
options.says: Ruled out because accuracy asks "Are the specific claims, figures, names, dates, quotations and citations true?", and every sentence here was true.

origin.section: Discern: four questions to ask of any output

questions.stem: A news desk asks Claude to confirm that a reader's photo of a flood is not AI-generated before it runs on the front page. What should the desk expect?

options.text: A confident answer once it has been asked to examine the image twice
options.says: Ruled out because "Always carefully review and verify Claude's image interpretations".

options.text: A reliable yes or no from the model after one look
options.says: Ruled out because "Do not use Claude for tasks requiring perfect precision or sensitive image analysis without human oversight".

options.text: No reliable verdict, so provenance checks and an editor decide
options.says: Claude cannot determine whether an image is AI-generated, so that judgement rests on other checks (module 4, page 1).

options.text: A refusal to look at the photo of a disaster
options.says: Ruled out because all current models "support text and image input".

questions.stem: A team lead skims Claude Tag's summary of a long thread, and also forwards a note that Claude drafted to a customer. How much reading does the page ask for in each case?

options.text: A light pass for both the digest and the note
options.says: Ruled out because "something going to a customer or changing a system gets a careful read".

options.text: A close read for both the digest and the note
options.says: Ruled out because "Do not check everything equally", so a summary does not get the close read that outgoing work does.

options.text: A close read for the digest, a light pass for the note to the customer
options.says: Ruled out because high stakes go to a human reviewer, including "anything sent externally in your organisation's name".

options.text: A light pass for the digest, a careful look at anything sent outside
options.says: The page asks to read Claude's work in proportion to what is at stake: a summary you can skim, and work going to a customer gets a careful read (module 8, page 2).

questions.stem: A test asserts that a Claude reply matches a stored string exactly. It passes today and fails tomorrow for the same input. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: The vendor swapped the model silently, so the id must be pinned and re-recorded
options.says: Ruled out because every id is pinned, "including the dateless IDs used from the 4.6 generation on".

options.text: Replies do vary even at fixed settings, so quality must be judged across many cases
options.says: Output varies by sampling and infrastructure, so one run proves nothing (module 1, page 2).

options.text: The prompt is faulty, and a line such as be consistent will stabilise it
options.says: Ruled out because "A prompt sentence does not remove sampling".

options.text: The machine's clock changed the output, so the time must be frozen
options.says: Ruled out because "The model has no clock", so freezing one changes nothing.

questions.stem: A clinic plans to have Claude read CT studies uploaded by patients and send the findings straight to them. Which concern matters most?

options.text: Cost: each scan would use too many visual tokens for the clinic's budget
options.says: Ruled out because Claude is "not designed to interpret complex diagnostic scans such as CTs or MRIs", whatever the cost or the image quality.

options.text: These scans lie outside the design, so a qualified reviewer must vet outputs
options.says: The vision limits include scans, and a decision reaching individuals needs a qualified reviewer (modules 4 and 10).

options.text: Naming: Claude would add the patients' names to its findings
options.says: Ruled out because "Claude cannot be used to name people in images, and refuses to".

options.text: Privacy: the scans would stay in the chat and surface in later conversations
options.says: Ruled out because "A conversation with Claude does not teach it anything that carries to the next conversation".

questions.stem: A knowledge-base assistant answers every question, even when the manuals say nothing, and sometimes invents a procedure. The manuals are already included with each request. Which prompt addition best tackles this?

options.text: Permission to admit that the text does not cover the case
options.says: Permission to say the material is insufficient is the first listed technique (module 1, page 2).

options.text: A lower temperature setting aimed at the guessing over missing steps
options.says: Ruled out because "The models this course uses do not accept them", and a setting does not give the model a way to say it does not know.

options.text: A confidence percentage placed beside each answer it gives
options.says: Ruled out because "asking a model how sure it is does not make a wrong answer right".

options.text: A second copy of the manuals at the end of each request
options.says: Ruled out because "accuracy and recall degrade, a phenomenon known as context rot", and the manuals are already supplied.

origin.section: What the current models let you set

questions.stem: A team sends Claude-drafted board papers weekly. Reviewers spend equal time on every sentence and still miss a wrong total. Which two changes fit? (Select two.)

options.text: Give each reviewer a longer checklist of style rules
options.says: Ruled out because "Readers check tone and grammar, which are visible", and skip the figures.

options.text: Ask Claude to mark the sentences it is least sure of and review only those
options.says: Ruled out because "Self-reported confidence is not a measure of accuracy".

options.text: Match effort to the cost of an error
options.says: Checking in proportion to the cost of being wrong puts the effort on figures and citations, because "You own what you send, whoever drafted it" (module 5, page 2).

options.text: Check nothing in routine papers once the author has read each draft
options.says: Ruled out because "A good draft does not show the figures were right".

options.text: Check figures and quotations first
options.says: Checking in proportion to the cost of being wrong puts the effort on figures and citations, because "You own what you send, whoever drafted it" (module 5, page 2).

questions.stem: An analyst asks Claude for the reasons a new policy will succeed, and the reply gives only supporters' views. The memo goes to a review committee. What is the best next step?

options.text: Ask Claude whether its answer was biased and accept the reply
options.says: Ruled out because asking the model "for its confidence does not verify anything".

options.text: Add a line to the memo saying that an AI drafted it
options.says: Ruled out because the fairness question is whether the output will "present one side as the whole", which a disclosure line leaves untouched.

options.text: Reword the request to cover each side's leading argument
options.says: Bias often comes from the framing of the request, so the request is revised and both framings are reviewed (module 5, page 2).

options.text: Switch to a larger tier and ask the same question again
options.says: Ruled out because "Bias in a response often comes from the framing of the request, so check the prompt as well as the answer".

questions.stem: A finance team plans to use Claude for Excel to produce the reconciliation that its auditors will rely on, and to send the result with no further checks. What does the add-in page say about this plan?

options.text: It is fine provided the workbook includes its macros for the whole reconciliation
options.says: Ruled out because "Macros and VBA, and data tables, are unsupported".

options.text: It is not advised for critical sign-off figures unless they are verified
options.says: The add-in page does not recommend relying on it for audit-critical calculations without verification (module 8, page 2).

options.text: It is fine when Claude is told to double-check its own totals before sending
options.says: Ruled out because "Self-reported confidence is not a measure of accuracy".

options.text: It is approved for such work thanks to the cell-level citations on each result
options.says: Ruled out because "a citation shows where an answer came from, not that the source is right".

questions.stem: Before sending a report to a client, an analyst asks Claude "How confident are you in these figures?" and gets "Very confident". Which view of that reply is right?

options.text: It lets the numbers skip review and go straight to the client
options.says: Ruled out because the page sends "anything sent externally in your organisation's name" to a human reviewer.

options.text: It proves nothing, so the numbers are checked against the data
options.says: Asking a model about its own certainty verifies nothing, so claims go to the source of record (module 5, page 2).

options.text: It is a good sign that the figures are right and complete
options.says: Ruled out because the page states "Confidence of tone is not a signal".

options.text: It settles the question of whether the figures are right
options.says: Ruled out because the page holds that "Self-reported confidence is not a measure of accuracy".

questions.stem: An analyst needs Claude's output to load into a database through a script, and also to show executives a short takeaway. Which pair of formats fits?

options.text: A published artifact with shared storage that serves both audiences at once
options.says: Ruled out because the warning is to "check whether the artifact uses shared storage" before sensitive entries.

options.text: An artifact for the ingest step, and a table in a slide deck for leadership
options.says: Ruled out because "Data that another program will read is structured data", not an artifact.

options.text: Inline replies for both audiences, with artifacts kept for code alone
options.says: Ruled out because an artifact suits "A document, deck, dashboard or small tool to hand to someone", not only code.

options.text: Machine-readable results for the ingest step, a brief inline note for leadership
options.says: Data a program reads is structured data, and a short takeaway stays inline (module 7, page 2).

origin.section: Artifacts: a deliverable beside the conversation

questions.stem: A communications assistant has Claude draft a press note that goes out under the organisation's name within the hour. It reports what the chief executive said and gives three percentages. What should be checked first?

options.text: Spelling and tone, read through line by line by a colleague
options.says: Ruled out because "Readers check tone and grammar, which are visible, and skip figures and citations, which are where the damage is".

options.text: The quotation and the statistics, against their originals
options.says: The claims that would hurt if wrong are checked against the source of record (module 5, page 2).

options.text: Each claim, against the confidence Claude states for it
options.says: Ruled out because "Self-reported confidence is not a measure of accuracy".

options.text: Each claim, against a second draft from Claude
options.says: Ruled out because the routine is "Check those against the source of record, not against the model".

questions.stem: A team runs Claude Haiku 4.5 on questions about product launches from mid-2025, and the answers are thin. Which fact from the models overview best accounts for this?

options.text: Its window is smaller than the others', so the later material no longer fits
options.says: Ruled out because the window is a "working memory", "different from the training data".

options.text: Its reliable knowledge is limited to February 2025, before those events took place
options.says: Haiku 4.5's reliable knowledge cutoff is February 2025, while the three larger models run to June 2026 (module 1, page 2).

options.text: Its training data cutoff is later than its reliable one, so it knows every event fully
options.says: Ruled out because the reliable date is "the date through which the model's knowledge is most extensive and reliable".

options.text: All tiers share the same dates, so switching tier could not change the result
options.says: Ruled out because the table gives "Claude Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 | June 2026 | June 2026".

origin.section: The context window is working memory

questions.stem: A retailer will draft about 5,000 short order-status replies an hour, and a few each hour need delicate judgment. Speed and cost matter most. What is the best opening move?

options.text: Use the middle tier until the invoices arrive, then decide
options.says: Ruled out because the decision rule is to "build benchmark tests for your use case", not wait for invoices.

options.text: Use the most capable tier for every reply to protect quality
options.says: Ruled out because "the top tier for everything wastes the budget".

options.text: Use the fast, cheap tier first and send hard cases higher
options.says: High-volume routine work starts on the efficient tier with the hard cases sent upward, and it is validated on real data (module 3, page 1).

options.text: Use the cheapest tier for every reply, hard cases included
options.says: Ruled out because "the cheapest model for everything under-serves exactly the cases that need depth".

origin.section: How the documentation says to choose

questions.stem: A team uses Claude Code in the terminal, and a colleague asks whether the repository's CLAUDE.md file and MCP servers also apply in the IDE extension and the desktop app. What does the surfaces page say?

options.text: They do, because every environment connects to the same underlying engine
options.says: Each surface connects to the same underlying Claude Code engine, so memory files, settings and MCP servers work across all of them (module 3, page 2).

options.text: They do not, since each surface keeps its own separate configuration files
options.says: Ruled out because Claude Code keeps "settings that travel with the repository across its surfaces".

options.text: They apply only in the terminal, since the files are read from a shell prompt
options.says: Ruled out because Claude Code is "available in the terminal, IDE extensions, a desktop app and the browser".

options.text: They apply only after being exported once into each of the other tools
options.says: Ruled out because "your repo's CLAUDE.md files, settings, and MCP servers work across all of them", with no export step.

origin.section: One model, many surfaces: what carries across

questions.stem: An analyst switches on Research mode to look up the notice period stated in a single contract that is already open. What does the course say about this choice?

options.text: It is more than the task needs, since one text answers it
options.says: Do not use Research for a question that one document answers (module 7, page 2).

options.text: It is the right choice, since contracts need many linked searches
options.says: Ruled out because "Use Research when the question is open and broad".

options.text: It is needed, since a notice period must be confirmed from web sources
options.says: Ruled out because "Do not use it for a question that one document answers, or one you can check in a minute" (module 7, page 2).

options.text: It is blocked, since Research cannot read a document that is already open
options.says: Ruled out because Research "draws on connected internal sources" as well as the web.

origin.section: Research: many linked searches, with citations

questions.stem: A long conversation in the app starts contradicting decisions made hours earlier, though no error appears. The lead wants the project to continue with every decision kept. Which action fits?

options.text: Ask Claude to restate every decision in the same conversation and continue
options.says: Ruled out because "accuracy and recall degrade, a phenomenon known as context rot", and a restatement inside the same long conversation leaves the degraded context in place.

options.text: Switch to a model with a larger window and continue in the same conversation
options.says: Ruled out because "Larger windows raise the ceiling; they do not remove the need to decide what goes in".

options.text: Begin a new chat with a short summary of the agreed points
options.says: A fresh start with a summary keeps the useful context and drops the rot (module 1, page 1).

options.text: Paste the whole earlier transcript into a new chat
options.says: Ruled out because "more context isn't automatically better", and the whole transcript brings the rot with it.

origin.section: More context is not automatically better

questions.stem: A strategist must compare twelve vendors using public sources and wants cited findings by tomorrow, with several rounds of investigation expected. Which feature fits best?

options.text: Research mode, with web search enabled
options.says: Research runs many linked searches with citations and needs web search on (module 7, page 2).

options.text: A Project loaded with each vendor's brochures
options.says: Ruled out because a Project suits "Recurring work with fixed rules and reference files".

options.text: A plain chat, asked for sources in each reply
options.says: Ruled out because plain chat is for "A one-off question, a draft, a quick comparison".

options.text: An artifact that lays the comparison out as a dashboard
options.says: Ruled out because an artifact is for "A document, deck, dashboard or small tool to hand to someone", not for gathering sources.

origin.section: Four questions that choose the surface

questions.stem: A team lists what to weigh before picking a model for a new feature. Which set matches the start of the "Choosing the right model" page?

options.text: What the task needs, the answer speed required, the cost, and the effort setting
options.says: The page starts with four criteria: capabilities (what the task needs), speed, cost and effort (module 3, page 1).

options.text: Brand, window size, release date and the number of supported languages
options.says: Ruled out because the page starts with "capabilities (what the task needs)", and brand and release date are not among its criteria.

options.text: Capabilities, speed, price and the cloud platform that hosts the model
options.says: Ruled out because the page ends its list with "cost (development and production), and effort", and names no hosting platform.

options.text: Latency, accuracy, safety and the vendor's retirement dates in the tables
options.says: Ruled out because the page's criteria include "cost (development and production)", which this set leaves out.

origin.section: How the documentation says to choose

questions.stem: A user tells Claude about a project in an incognito chat and finds that the next chat has no trace of it. Which two statements are correct? (Select two.)

options.text: A Project would have remembered everything the user said
options.says: Ruled out because "Each project has its own separate memory space and dedicated project summary".

options.text: The weights should have updated after the exchange
options.says: Ruled out because "Weights are fixed at inference time".

options.text: The behaviour is intended and not a fault
options.says: Incognito chats "keep a conversation out of memory and history" on purpose (modules 7 and 10).

options.text: Incognito chats can only be started inside a Project
options.says: Ruled out because "Incognito chats are available only outside Projects" (module 7, page 1), so one cannot be started inside a Project.

options.text: That mode is built to bypass memory and history
options.says: Incognito chats "keep a conversation out of memory and history" on purpose (modules 7 and 10).

questions.stem: An FP&A analyst must trace how a revenue figure in a long workbook is derived before presenting it. Which capability of the Excel add-in helps most directly?

options.text: Reading closed workbooks stored in the shared drive
options.says: Ruled out because "Claude can read and write only files that are open at that moment".

options.text: Automatic sign-off of the figure by the add-in once it is asked
options.says: Ruled out because it is "Not recommended for final client deliverables without human review".

options.text: Answers about the open file that carry cell-level citations
options.says: The add-in answers with clickable cell-level citations (module 8, page 2).

options.text: Macro execution that recalculates the whole workbook automatically
options.says: Ruled out because "Macros and VBA, and data tables, are unsupported".

questions.stem: A sales team's lead has one skill for proposal layouts that works well and now wants the team's connectors and several other playbooks packaged for a regular role. What does the course suggest?

options.text: Upload each playbook as its own skill and leave the connectors out
options.says: Ruled out because "a plugin bundles skills, connectors and sub-agents around a job".

options.text: Test the first piece, then scale it into a shared plugin
options.says: The Academy lesson recommends starting with one skill, testing it and then scaling to a plugin you share (module 8, page 1).

options.text: Build the whole plugin first and test each skill after rollout
options.says: Ruled out because the lesson recommends "starting with one skill, testing it and then scaling to a plugin you share" (module 8, page 1), so testing comes before the plugin and not after rollout.

options.text: Keep the one skill and put the connectors in the Project's instructions
options.says: Ruled out because "Where a skill is one playbook, a plugin is several, plus the connectors they depend on".

questions.stem: A small charity asks Claude for a first draft of a grant application and receives polished text in a corporate voice that misses the funder's priorities. Which two statements fit the course's guidance for this audience? (Select two.)

options.text: The request should give only a word limit and a deadline, judged on form alone
options.says: Ruled out because "If they would need to ask you a question before starting, the model needs the answer in the prompt", and a newcomer would first ask what the funder wants.

options.text: The request should list the donor's criteria
options.says: A non-profit describes the funder's criteria, its mission and voice, the audience and the facts that must appear, and avoids "Stacking adjectives instead of constraints" (module 9, page 2).

options.text: It should also give the mission, tone and reader
options.says: A non-profit describes the funder's criteria, its mission and voice, the audience and the facts that must appear, and avoids "Stacking adjectives instead of constraints" (module 9, page 2).

options.text: The request should list warm, moving and professional adjectives for the whole text
options.says: Ruled out because a string of adjectives like "Be concise, thorough, clear and professional" "gives conflicting, unverifiable demands".

options.text: The request should ask it to sound like a larger charity with a longer record
options.says: Ruled out because the officer checks "whether a draft overstates what the programme achieved".

questions.stem: An online shop wants every order with a postcode outside its delivery zones flagged automatically, and 12,000 orders arrive daily. Which design is best?

options.text: Claude drafts customer notes while a short program applies the geographic rule
options.says: A rule that fits in one line belongs in code (module 4, page 2).

options.text: Claude reads each order and decides whether the postcode lies out of zone

options.text: Claude checks a sample of orders and the rest are assumed to be fine
options.says: Ruled out because "A prompt is a request, not a guarantee", and a sample leaves the rest unchecked.

options.text: Claude flags suspicious postcodes by feel, then code confirms them

origin.section: When not to use a model

questions.stem: When choosing between Claude surfaces, a team ranks options by power. The course gives a different principle behind its table of what each surface must not be given. What is it?

options.text: Most action, with an approval step that only slows the task
options.says: Ruled out because "Prefer a surface and an approval mode where a person confirms the consequential steps".

options.text: Least reach, least action, and most visibility for the right people
options.says: The pattern is least reach, least action, and most visibility to the right people (module 8, page 3).

options.text: Maximum reach, with no second surface ever needed for the work
options.says: Ruled out because "Picking the most powerful surface" is named as a trap.

options.text: Least visibility, with results kept private to the person asking
options.says: Ruled out because "Ignoring who sees the result" is named as a trap.

origin.section: Four questions that choose the surface

questions.stem: A COO asks which of four chores suit Claude with review and no extra tools: (1) drafting vendor-email variants, (2) making the final call on which supplier to drop, (3) summarising call transcripts, (4) calculating invoice totals to the cent in the chat. Which pair is right?

options.text: The second and fourth
options.says: Ruled out because chore 2 needs "judgment that carries accountability", and chore 4 needs exactness.

options.text: The first and third
options.says: Chores 1 and 3 are language-shaped work that a review can catch, while the supplier decision and exact sums are not (module 5, page 1).

options.text: The third and fourth
options.says: Ruled out because chore 4, the totals, needs "exactness (money, counts, identifiers)".

options.text: The first and second
options.says: Ruled out because "A step stays with a person, or with code" when it needs accountable judgment such as the supplier decision in chore 2.

origin.section: Delegate: which steps go to Claude

questions.stem: A department head must explain to staff what Claude changes in the team's work. Which message has all three parts of the course's structure?

options.text: It speeds first drafts and summaries, and people still check claims and decisions
options.says: Ruled out because the message must also say "how you will know it works (a spot-check rate, an example set, a before and after on time)".

options.text: It speeds drafts and summaries, people still check claims, results get measured
options.says: A fair message says what it speeds up, what still needs a person and how the team will know it works (module 5, page 2).

options.text: People still check claims and decisions, and we will measure spot-check rates
options.says: Ruled out because the message must also say "what it speeds up (first drafts, summaries, comparisons, variations)".

options.text: It handles drafts and summaries, and review can shrink once the first month looks clean
options.says: Ruled out because "A good draft does not show the figures were right", so review cannot shrink on a clean run.

origin.section: Explaining value and limits to colleagues

questions.stem: A product team asks Claude for "a settings page" and receives a generic design that breaks an existing layout. Which two statements match how the course says a builder should describe the job? (Select two.)

options.text: Add more adjectives about the style and mood of the page
options.says: Ruled out because the page names "Stacking adjectives instead of constraints" as a trap.

options.text: Name what must stay as it is
options.says: A builder describes "the problem and the constraints, not only the task" (module 9, page 1): who the user is, what exists, what must not change and what done looks like.

options.text: Say who will use it and what is already built
options.says: A builder describes "the problem and the constraints, not only the task" (module 9, page 1): who the user is, what exists, what must not change and what done looks like.

options.text: Give only the task and let a strong model infer the rest
options.says: Ruled out because "If they would need to ask you a question before starting, the model needs the answer in the prompt".

options.text: Ask for three finished designs in one go for comparison
options.says: Ruled out because "Start narrow, learn how Claude does on your material, then widen".

questions.stem: A lecturer designs a take-home essay brief and wonders whether students could simply paste it into an AI. Which check does the course list for educators?

options.text: If the brief is long enough to need several drafts from each student
options.says: Ruled out because educators check "accuracy of the content taught, bias or stereotypes in examples, reading level, alignment with the stated outcome".

options.text: If students are told which model the lecturer used to prepare it
options.says: Ruled out because "Names, grades and records fall under the organisation's rules".

options.text: If the rubric is written by Claude and then checked once by hand
options.says: Ruled out because the educator "Owns: what students are taught, how they are assessed and the fairness of grades".

options.text: If a chatbot could finish the task unaided, and if that matters
options.says: Educators check whether an assignment can be completed by pasting it into an AI, and whether that matters (module 9, page 1).

questions.stem: A shop's support inbox gets about 300 routine order questions a day, plus occasional warranty and refund disputes, and nobody reviews the answers sent today. Which workflow change fits?

options.text: Draft everything on the top tier and send the replies out automatically
options.says: Ruled out because "the top tier for everything wastes the budget", and nothing stops an unchecked commitment.

options.text: Draft everything on a fast tier and spot-check the results, disputes included as well
options.says: Ruled out because "a contract, a legal term or a customer's money does not go out on trust".

options.text: Keep the replies manual and use Claude only to correct their spelling
options.says: Ruled out because "High-volume, low-stakes drafting suits a faster, cheaper model" with a spot check, so manual work throws the benefit away.

options.text: Spot-checked fast-tier drafts, with a person signing off any reply that commits money
options.says: High-volume low-stakes drafting suits a faster, cheaper model with a spot check, and a customer's money does not go out on trust (module 9, page 2).

questions.stem: A Team plan owner wants every member to have the company's brand-writing skill without each uploading it, while letting members switch it off. Which kind of skill fits?

options.text: A centrally provisioned one with a toggle for each person
options.says: Organisation skills are provisioned by Team and Enterprise owners to every member, who can toggle them (module 7, page 2).

options.text: A custom skill that each person builds and uploads alone
options.says: Ruled out because a custom skill is "Yours or your organisation's: brand rules, a meeting-notes format, a recurring analysis".

options.text: A partner skill, written to work with another firm's connectors
options.says: Ruled out because partner skills come "From other companies, built to work with their connectors".

options.text: An Anthropic skill, which is built in for office and PDF files
options.says: Ruled out because those are "Built in, for creating Excel, Word, PowerPoint and PDF files".

origin.section: Skills: a playbook Claude loads when it is relevant

questions.stem: A Project's HR assistant quotes a leave policy that was replaced, and both the old and the new document sit in its knowledge. Compliance wants the prior edition to stay retrievable for audits. What is the best fix?

options.text: Ask Claude to merge both files into a third file and use that one
options.says: Ruled out because "Judge the source before you add it", and a merged file adds a new unchecked source.

options.text: Keep both and add an instruction to prefer the newer document when they conflict
options.says: Ruled out because "an instruction is a request and a deleted file is a guarantee", so the conflict stays possible.

options.text: Take the outdated file out of the workspace and archive it in your own storage
options.says: A deleted file is a guarantee, and the archived copy in your own storage meets the audit need (module 7, page 1).

options.text: Switch on memory, which lets Claude learn which policy is current
options.says: Ruled out because "memory is not a substitute for a knowledge file".

questions.stem: A team wants every Claude Tag reply in one Slack channel to be brief and to link its source. Which two statements describe the setup? (Select two.)

options.text: Ask each member to retype the rule in every thread
options.says: Ruled out because "You can set a channel's standing instructions by telling Claude there", so members need not repeat them in every thread.

options.text: Set it in a Project, whose instructions Slack reads first
options.says: Ruled out because "Project instructions apply to every chat in that Project".

options.text: Lower the temperature in the model's settings
options.says: Ruled out because "The models this course uses do not accept them".

options.text: Admins can review and delete what is stored
options.says: Standing instructions "go to channel memory, which admins can review and delete" (module 8, page 2).

options.text: Say it to the assistant where the replies appear
options.says: Standing instructions "go to channel memory, which admins can review and delete" (module 8, page 2).

questions.stem: A team lead wants the whole organisation to use a Project of staff guidance, but salary bands may be seen only by the HR group. Which approach is right?

options.text: Share one Project widely and tell its instructions to withhold the salary bands
options.says: Ruled out because the guidance is "Treat sharing as publishing", and an instruction is a request.

options.text: Share one Project widely with view-only access, which keeps viewers out of the knowledge
options.says: Ruled out because can view gives "read-only access to contents, knowledge and instructions", which is reading.

options.text: Share one Project widely now, and delete the salary bands later if anyone objects
options.says: Ruled out because "anyone with access can read the instructions and every file in the knowledge base", and deleting later does not undo that.

options.text: Share the other material widely after moving the confidential figures to an HR-only area
options.says: Sharing shows the instructions and every file to everyone with access, so the bands live in a separate Project that only HR can open (module 7, page 1).

questions.stem: A team syncs a Google document that holds a pasted chart image with the key figures into a private Project. Answers ignore those figures. Which limit explains it?

options.text: The Project reached its context limit, so retrieval skipped the chart
options.says: Ruled out because retrieval starts "when a Project approaches the context limit", and that does not explain missing images.

options.text: The sync copies only the first page of each document into the Project
options.says: Ruled out because the page says "images embedded in a document are not processed", and states no page limit.

options.text: The connector reads text only, so embedded pictures are not processed
options.says: The Drive connector reads text content only, and images embedded in a document are not processed (module 7, page 1).

options.text: A private Project cannot sync from Drive at all, so the chart was never read
options.says: Ruled out because "a Drive document added to a private Project's knowledge syncs from Drive".

origin.section: How much fits: context and retrieval

questions.stem: A policy exists in the company wiki and as a PDF inside a Project. After two quarters the two differ, and Claude quotes both. Which principle of keeping knowledge current was missed?

options.text: Version names added to the title of every file in the Project
options.says: Ruled out because the advice to "Put a version or date in the file name and the first line" helps you go back, and does not stop two live sources.

options.text: Source judgement applied before anything is uploaded to the Project
options.says: Ruled out because that principle is to "prefer the final approved text over a draft", which is about quality.

options.text: A review date written on each document that the Project holds
options.says: Ruled out because a review date makes "a stale file is a missed appointment, not a surprise", and does not remove the duplicate.

options.text: A single source of record, mirrored by the workspace or synced directly
options.says: Keep one source of record: if the policy exists in the wiki and as a PDF in the Project, one of them is wrong within a quarter (module 7, page 1).

questions.stem: A coordinator builds a small published artifact where parents of pupils enter their children's dietary needs, and it keeps data. What should the coordinator check before inviting people?

options.text: Whether its storage is personal or visible to every user
options.says: Shared storage is visible to every user, so check it before sensitive entries (module 7, page 2).

options.text: Whether the artifact runs past fifteen lines, which decides its storage
options.says: Ruled out because the fifteen-line figure is about when an artifact is made, "typically over 15 lines, and reusable on its own".

options.text: Whether each visitor has the creator's plan, with usage billed to it
options.says: Ruled out because "Their use counts against their own plan limits, not the creator's".

options.text: Whether visitors have connected the creator's own apps
options.says: Ruled out because "each person connects their own apps even in a shared artifact".

origin.section: Artifacts: a deliverable beside the conversation

questions.stem: A researcher replaces patient names with codes and keeps the table of codes in a locked folder. The data also lists a rare job title, a small town and an exact visit date. Is it now anonymous?

options.text: No, but only because the exact date is present, so drop that single field
options.says: Ruled out because the page says "a rare job title, a small town and an exact date can identify a person without a name".

options.text: Yes, because the table that reverses the codes is stored apart and locked
options.says: Ruled out because the page states "Pseudonymised data is still personal data under many rules".

options.text: No, since the mix is still identifying, so generalise it further
options.says: A rare combination can identify a person without a name, so the data is generalised further (module 10, page 1).

options.text: Yes, since coding is the strongest technique on the list of methods in use
options.says: Ruled out because the list of techniques runs from strongest to weakest, and it starts with "Aggregate. Send totals and trends, not rows".

questions.stem: A member of a Team plan finds that memory and a particular connector are missing from their settings, while a friend at another company has both. Which two statements explain it? (Select two.)

options.text: The source system blocks anything absent from a personal allow list
options.says: Ruled out because "an owner must enable connectors for the organisation before members can use them".

options.text: Features stay hidden until each member opts in individually
options.says: Ruled out because "Owners enable connectors, memory, skills and other features for the organisation; members cannot use what is off" (module 10, page 2), so no member can opt in alone.

options.text: The account owners switch features on or off
options.says: "Owners enable connectors, memory, skills and other features for the organisation; members cannot use what is off" (module 10, page 2).

options.text: Individuals cannot override those switches
options.says: "Owners enable connectors, memory, skills and other features for the organisation; members cannot use what is off" (module 10, page 2).

options.text: A line manager can override any setting in a member's workspace
options.says: Ruled out because "the people who run the organisation hold settings that individuals cannot override".

questions.stem: A team on a commercial plan asks whether Anthropic may use its inputs to build better models, and how long chats are kept. Which answer is accurate?

options.text: They are used unless an owner opts out, and they are then kept for up to five years
options.says: Ruled out because "By default Anthropic does not use inputs or outputs from commercial products to train models".

options.text: They are never used, and they are always deleted the moment a chat comes to an end
options.says: Ruled out because "Inputs and outputs are deleted within 30 days by default", not at once.

options.text: They are used only if each member allows it in their own privacy settings
options.says: Ruled out because the choice in privacy settings is the consumer rule, while commercial plans start from "does not use inputs or outputs from commercial products to train models".

options.text: They are not used by default, and are deleted within 30 days unless custom or zero retention applies
options.says: Commercial products are not used to train models by default, and data is deleted within 30 days by default (module 10, page 1).

origin.section: What happens to what you type

questions.stem: A manager connects a client folder to Cowork and is concerned that a task might remove files. What does the safety page say about permanent deletion?

options.text: Claude cannot delete anything from the connected folder
options.says: Ruled out because "Claude can read, write and permanently delete files in the folders you connect".

options.text: Claude deletes silently once the folder is connected
options.says: Ruled out because "It needs your explicit permission before a permanent deletion".

options.text: Explicit permission comes first, and key material should be backed up
options.says: Claude needs explicit permission before a permanent deletion, and the page says to keep backups of important files (module 8, page 1).

options.text: Backups are unnecessary once permission has been given for the removal
options.says: Ruled out because "you should keep backups of important files".

origin.section: Safe use: what the help centre asks of you

questions.stem: A researcher must report survey findings by area and age group, and policy restricts personal data. The responses include names and a free-text column. Which preparation is best?

options.text: Delete only the names column and upload the rest, trusting open text to be anonymous
options.says: Ruled out because "Notes columns hide names and details".

options.text: Coarsen places and ages into bands, strip identities, and read the open answers
options.says: Generalise, and check free text, which hides details (module 10, page 1).

options.text: Replace each name with a code and keep the key list in the same file
options.says: Ruled out because "Pseudonymised data is still personal data under many rules, because the key can reverse it".

options.text: Upload everything and ask for a summary that leaves out personal details
options.says: Ruled out because asking for a summary without personal details "is a request, and it does not satisfy a policy control".

questions.stem: A manager lets Cowork reach an entire documents drive to save time, and it holds tax returns and exported passwords. Which two changes fit? (Select two.)

options.text: Use manual approval for sensitive material
options.says: A dedicated working folder limits what a mistake or an injected instruction can reach, and the habit is to "use Manual approval for sensitive files, new tools and hard-to-undo actions" (module 8, page 1).

options.text: Connect a dedicated folder with only the needed items
options.says: A dedicated working folder limits what a mistake or an injected instruction can reach, and the habit is to "use Manual approval for sensitive files, new tools and hard-to-undo actions" (module 8, page 1).

options.text: Keep the access but ask Claude to ignore the sensitive items
options.says: Ruled out because the habit is to "grant access selectively and avoid financial documents, credentials and personal records".

options.text: Keep the access and rely on the cloud sandbox
options.says: Ruled out because the isolation "doesn't limit what Claude reads or does" through connected tools.

options.text: Keep the access but switch to automatic approval for speed
options.says: Ruled out because Auto only has Claude check each action, and "it still runs on its own".

origin.section: Safe use: what the help centre asks of you

questions.stem: A professional asks Claude in Chrome to shortlist conference venues while a banking site is open in another tab, with ten minutes left before a call. Which habit best limits harm?

options.text: Rely on the classifiers, which screen each action
options.says: Ruled out because the page says plainly that "the risk is not zero".

options.text: Leave the bank tab open but ask Claude to skip it
options.says: Ruled out because "whatever is visible in them becomes part of the conversation".

options.text: Switch on Skip all approvals, with no prompt interrupting the task
options.says: Ruled out because in that mode "Claude does not pause and nothing checks its actions".

options.text: Use a clean profile, and approve each action manually
options.says: A separate profile and manual approval limit what Claude can see and do (module 8, page 2).

questions.stem: A company approved a remote tool for Claude a year ago, and its provider has since changed hands. Nobody has looked at its connector list since. Which governance step was skipped?

options.text: A switch to a custom connector, which Anthropic has verified
options.says: Ruled out because "a custom connector has not been verified by Anthropic".

options.text: A periodic review of what is linked, with trust given at install treated as aging
options.says: Remote tools can change after you approve them, so the connector list is reviewed on a schedule (module 7, page 3).

options.text: A one-time classification of the tool's data, valid while it stays in use
options.says: Ruled out because the checklist says "Review the list on a schedule", which a one-time classification is not.

options.text: A stronger approval prompt for each single call to the tool
options.says: Ruled out because the checklist says "re-check the ones whose provider changed".

questions.stem: A student submits an essay drafted entirely by Claude to a course whose rules require AI help to be declared, and does not declare it. Which Usage Policy category does this touch?

options.text: A high-risk use of the model in a regulated professional field
options.says: Ruled out because the policy singles out "uses where output directly affects individuals or consumers".

options.text: Fraudulent, abusive or predatory practices, like unattributed AI work
options.says: The Usage Policy lists plagiarising or submitting AI-assisted work without proper permission or attribution under fraudulent, abusive or predatory practices (module 10, page 1).

options.text: Compromising privacy or identity of the people the essay names
options.says: Ruled out because that category covers "sharing personal information without consent".

options.text: Misinformation spread to the public through the essay itself
options.says: Ruled out because that category is "creating or spreading misinformation, including false medical or scientific information and impersonation".

origin.section: The Usage Policy in three parts

questions.stem: A team's bill jumps after it starts sending full-size phone photos with each request, though the text prompts are unchanged. Which two facts about images explain the jump? (Select two.)

options.text: Photos are turned into text first, which multiplies the words sent
options.says: Ruled out because "Claude reads images and PDFs" directly, so photos are not turned into text first.

options.text: Large pictures use many tokens, up to a model's cap
options.says: Each 28 by 28 pixel patch is one visual token, so an image costs "about ceil(width/28) x ceil(height/28) tokens up to a per-model cap" (module 4, page 1).

options.text: Images count toward the window but are never billed as input
options.says: Ruled out because "Images also cost tokens", and tokens are what is billed as input.

options.text: Each 28 by 28 pixel patch is a token
options.says: Each 28 by 28 pixel patch is one visual token, so an image costs "about ceil(width/28) x ceil(height/28) tokens up to a per-model cap" (module 4, page 1).

options.text: Images are priced as a flat fee that ignores their size
options.says: Ruled out because "A 1000 by 1000 image is 1,296 tokens", a count that depends on the size.

questions.stem: An analyst asks the Excel add-in to recalculate a what-if data table and to edit a VBA macro in the same workbook, and both requests fail. What explains it?

options.text: The add-in needs an Enterprise plan before it can edit macros
options.says: Ruled out because the add-ins are "installed from Microsoft AppSource, for the paid plans".

options.text: The workbook is too large, so Claude splits it and skips those parts
options.says: Ruled out because "Macros and VBA, and data tables, are unsupported".

options.text: Neither is supported by this tool, so those parts stay manual
options.says: The page lists macros and VBA, and data tables, as unsupported (module 8, page 2).

options.text: Cross-app work is switched off, which blocks edits to every sheet
options.says: Ruled out because cross-app work concerns files and uses "Let Claude work across files".

questions.stem: A nightly job summarises 3,000 documents. The output is good, but the bill is above budget and the run finishes after the morning deadline. Which plan fits the course's method?

options.text: Rewrite the instructions, add examples and change tier together, then compare
options.says: Ruled out because the habit is to "Change one thing at a time and re-run the same test inputs".

options.text: Move every document to the lower tier and ship the results without testing
options.says: Ruled out because "Having a good evaluation set is the most important step".

options.text: Raise effort to the maximum, with fewer retries expected as a result
options.says: Ruled out because effort "trades intelligence for latency and cost within a single model", and a maximum setting adds both.

options.text: Name the cause, try one lower-cost faster tier on the same test set, and compare
options.says: The method is to diagnose first, change one thing and compare on the same inputs, and a faster lower-cost tier answers both the bill and the deadline.

questions.stem: A nightly job re-scores 200,000 archived documents, and the results are due the next morning. Which cost lever fits best?

options.text: Batched requests, which are half the price of standard ones
options.says: Latency-tolerant bulk work suits batches, which are 50 percent cheaper (module 3, page 1).

options.text: Prompt cache reads, which price every output token lower
options.says: Ruled out because cache reads are described as costing "a fraction of the base input price", and these documents are all different.

options.text: Fast mode, which doubles the output speed at premium pricing
options.says: Ruled out because fast mode offers "up to 2.5x higher output speed at premium pricing", which raises cost.

options.text: Higher effort, which trades latency for cost
options.says: Ruled out because effort "trades intelligence for latency and cost within a single model", not bulk cost.

questions.stem: A support bot resends the same 40,000-token manual with every turn, and the bill is far higher than expected. Which lever does Level 1 name for reusing context instead of resending it?

options.text: Prompt caching in the API, or a Project's stored material in the apps
options.says: Reusing context instead of resending it is what Projects in the apps and caching in the API are for (module 6, page 4).

options.text: A higher output limit, which spreads the cost across more tokens
options.says: Ruled out because "max_tokens is a cap on output, not on context".

options.text: A larger context window, on the idea that more room makes each request cheaper
options.says: Ruled out because "If the same document is re-sent on every turn of that conversation, its cost is paid again each time".

options.text: A lower temperature, which shortens the manual that is sent
options.says: Ruled out because "The models this course uses do not accept them".

questions.stem: A model gives correct, well-formatted labels but is too slow for a live widget, and the labels must stay as accurate as today. The instructions and context are good. Which step fits?

options.text: Cut the instructions to a single line to save processing time
options.says: Ruled out because the table describes this case as "Correct instructions, correct context, still a capability or speed miss".

options.text: Add three more examples so the model answers more briefly
options.says: Ruled out because "every example is tokens in every request", which adds delay.

options.text: Test a faster tier or lower effort on the same set of cases
options.says: Correct instructions and context with a speed miss point to another tier or lower effort, tested on the same set (module 6, page 4).

options.text: Turn off thinking everywhere and ship without re-running the tests
options.says: Ruled out because the habit is to "Change one thing at a time and re-run the same test inputs".
